faq: What does this tool calculate?
The calendar date and clock time a Unix timestamp (seconds since the 1970 epoch, UTC) corresponds to, rendered in a chosen local zone and in UTC.
Do I need an account?
No — number in, moment out.
Can I use the result for professional work?
Yes — it is the standard conversion, zone-explicit. Incident reports live or die on stated zones; this page states them.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — the zone is chosen by you; nothing detects it.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Zone names are the IANA database's; renderings agree on the instant even when labels differ.
The year is absurd.
Your timestamp is probably milliseconds (13 digits) or microseconds (16). Scale it to seconds and convert again.
Negative timestamps?
Pre-1970 instants convert correctly — history is valid input.
What about the 2038 problem?
32-bit signed timestamps overflow at 2,147,483,647 (January 19, 2038). This converter's arithmetic is not 32-bit; the embedded systems in your life may be — the conversion exposes their cliff edge.
Leap seconds?
Unix time smooths them away by design; the rendered clock time follows civil time as the tz database states it.
Birthdates before 1970?
Negative timestamps render correctly — a 1965 birthdate is a routine conversion, and the converter's table stakes.
The timestamp has decimals.
Sub-second precision: the whole seconds convert here; the fraction rides along unchanged. Precision is preserved by not rounding what you were given.
